extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, mathematics students, educators, and members of the mathematical community (MAA/AMS readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and informal standards for living and working as a professional mathematician, drawn from Paul Halmos's advice and life: attitudes, teaching, talks, advising, writing, community engagement, and departmental culture. Presented as a DVD review summarizing Halmos's prescriptions and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal disposition and commitment
rubrics_metrics.description: You have to be born right, you must continually strive to become perfect, you must love mathematics more than anything else, you must work at it hard and without stop, and you must never give up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Halmos frames being a mathematician as an all-encompassing vocation or lifestyle rather than merely a job — social, professional, family, friends, and travel were all informed by mathematics in his life. The review presents this as a central (if somewhat old-fashioned) prescription for becoming a mathematician.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immersion in mathematical community and daily engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize and attend daily mathematical lunches, teas, colloquia, regional workshops, and social events; make colleagues close friends and participate in departmental social life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Halmos modeled a life of frequent, informal mathematical interaction (banging on doors with his cane to gather people for lunch, attending most colloquia, going to workshops, hosting social events mixing mathematicians and other intellectuals). The review highlights this community immersion as a key part of professional development and intellectual life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talks should present proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Every talk should contain a proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as a Halmos prescription for mathematical talks — talks should not be purely survey or rhetorical but include substantive mathematical argument (a proof) to demonstrate content and rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching by questioning (pedagogical method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching should be about asking questions, not giving answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review notes Halmos's enthusiasm for the Moore method (student discovery via questions/problems) while also acknowledging he was a superb lecturer and that the Moore method did not exclusively define his teaching. Emphasis is on pedagogy that encourages student thinking rather than simply delivering answers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advising: get students started by suggesting problems
rubrics_metrics.description: The hardest part about being an advisor is to get a student started—to suggest a problem for the student to work on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Halmos regarded the advisor's crucial early role as helping students begin research by proposing accessible problems; launching a student into active work is emphasized over other mentoring tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters of recommendation: truthful but calibrated
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters of recommendation should be governed by two rules: always tell the truth, but sometimes not the whole truth; and no matter how much good you want to say, be sure to say something bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Halmos advocates candor tempered with professional calibration: be honest but recognize rhetorical/contextual constraints; include at least one critical or tempering remark so the letter remains believable and informative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expository writing and surveys: strive for excellent exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Surveys are hard to write, but good expositions—the low road—are harder still. A good book review is a chatty expository essay on a currently interesting subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Halmos values clear, accessible exposition and sees high-quality expository writing as a demanding craft. Book reviews should be conversational expositions that illuminate an important topic rather than mere summaries or critiques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Departmental evaluation includes social interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: When job candidates came for interviews, the whole department was part of the evaluation process, including (often) at meals and social gatherings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review notes an older norm where candidate assessment included observations during informal settings; this implies professional demeanor, collegiality, and social fit are part of hiring judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead by organizing and cultivating interdisciplinary social events
rubrics_metrics.description: Hold social events that mix mathematicians, historians, philosophers, and musicians together; attend parties for speakers and candidates; create inclusive social spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Halmos's practice of hosting and attending varied intellectual social gatherings is presented as a model for fostering intellectual cross-pollination and a vibrant departmental culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional activities span writing, talking, publishing, traveling, teaching, and editing
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematician's professional duties include writing, talking, publishing, traveling, teaching, editing, and many other activities mathematicians engage in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The DVD and accompanying scanned writings highlight that professional excellence involves mastery of multiple roles (researcher, expositor, editor, traveler, teacher) and attention to craft in each area.
